name: HiAgent

paper.title: HiAgent: Hierarchical Working Memory Management for Solving Long-Horizon Agent Tasks with Large Language Model

construction.unit: subgoal chunk: an LLM-written subgoal plus the action-observation pairs taken under it
construction.kept_as: current subgoal's pairs verbatim; each finished subgoal as subgoal + LLM summary
construction.processing: the LLM writes a subgoal before acting; when it opens the next one, the finished chunk is shown as subgoal + summarized observation
construction.writer: backbone LLM (gpt-4-turbo) for subgoals and summaries

organization.structure: two levels inside one trial: numbered subgoals, each holding its action-observation pairs
organization.stores: one in-trial history list; raw pairs of finished subgoals kept but hidden from the prompt

management.operations: replace a finished chunk's pairs by its summary in the prompt; retrieve(id) shows the pairs again until the next subgoal
management.forgetting: nothing deleted; code drops the oldest entries when the prompt exceeds the 8,192-token window

retrieval.query: agent emits retrieve(subgoal_id, ...) as an action
retrieval.selection: the agent chooses which ids to expand
retrieval.budget: no cap on ids; expansion lasts until a new subgoal is written (code)

use.context: instruction + 1 in-context example + past subgoals with summaries + current subgoal's full pairs
use.reasoning: one LLM call per step outputs an action, or a new subgoal and its first action

classify.note: Memory is the in-trial context only. A finished subgoal's pairs are folded into a summary in the prompt; the agent re-expands a subgoal by id, so the lookup is by number, not by similarity.

stages.ingestion: Every environment observation is appended, with the action that caused it, to the chunk of the current subgoal.
stages.construction: Before acting, the LLM writes a subgoal; its actions and observations form one chunk. When the LLM judges the subgoal done it writes the next subgoal together with its first action.
stages.organization: Working memory is a two-level list: numbered past subgoals, each shown with a summarized observation, then the current subgoal with all of its pairs.
stages.update: A finished chunk's pairs are replaced in the prompt by an LLM summary that also states whether the subgoal was met; the raw pairs stay in the history.
stages.retrieval: When the LLM outputs retrieve(id), the pairs of that past subgoal are put back into the prompt in place of its summary, until a new subgoal is written.
stages.answer: Each step one LLM call reads the instruction, one in-context example and the working memory and outputs the next action.

summary: Working-memory manager for long agent tasks: the LLM writes subgoals as memory chunks, finished chunks are shown only as subgoal + summary, and the agent can re-expand a past chunk by id.

headline: The memory lives only inside one trial: it is the agent's own prompt, reorganized by subgoal.
A finished subgoal's action-observation pairs leave the prompt and are replaced by a short summary; the raw pairs are kept and can be re-expanded by id.
In the released code Blocksworld and Gripper never call the summarizer: a finished subgoal shows only its last observation.

abstract.text: HiAgent targets the in-trial (working) memory of LLM agents on long tasks, where the usual practice feeds every past action and observation back into the prompt. The agent is prompted to write a subgoal before acting and to treat each subgoal as a memory chunk. When it moves to a new subgoal, the finished chunk is shown only as the subgoal and a summarized observation, and the agent can ask to see a past chunk's full trajectory again. On five long-horizon AgentBoard tasks with GPT-4 the authors report twice the success rate of the standard full-history prompt, 3.8 fewer steps and about a third less context.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on the ACL Anthology page.

open_questions: If the released code matches the paper runs, Blocksworld and Gripper results are the 'w/o OS' configuration, so the Table 2 ablation (run on Tyreworld only) does not describe those two tasks.
Summaries are recomputed for every past subgoal each time the prompt is built, but the run-time comparison (80.58%) does not separate agent calls from summarizer calls.
How often the agent calls retrieve(...) is not reported.

The agent can output retrieve(id) to swap a past subgoal's summary for its raw pairs, which stay visible until it writes the next subgoal.

key_numbers.value: gpt-4-turbo, same as the agent; off for Blocksworld and Gripper in code

components.role: Writes subgoals, acts, asks to retrieve

ablation.src: paper Table 2 and Table 3, Tyreworld only (gpt-4-turbo). *Table 3 gives Context and Time relative to STANDARD, Table 2 relative to HiAgent.

discussion.takeaway: Treating subgoals as memory chunks, and showing only a summary of each finished one, lets a GPT-4 agent finish long planning tasks more often, in fewer steps and with less context, than feeding it the full history.

claims.claim: HiAgent doubles the success rate of the full-history STANDARD prompt.
claims.evidence: Average success 42.00 vs 21.00 and progress 62.55 vs 38.61 over five tasks; Table 1, §4.2
3.80 fewer steps, context 64.98% and run time 80.58% of STANDARD; Table 1
Tyreworld success 60.0 vs 30.0 without summarization and 50.0 without retrieval; Table 2, §5.1

claims.claim: The gain is not only from task decomposition.
claims.evidence: Subgoals without hiding past pairs reach 40.0 success on Tyreworld vs 60.0 for HiAgent, with 112.8% context; Table 3, §5.3
Wilcoxon signed-rank: progress rate p = 2.38e-5, steps p = 0.0016; §5.5

limits: Very long tasks may still exceed memory limits despite the shorter context.
Better retrieval strategies are left to future work.
Experiments cover benchmark tasks only, not real-world applications.
reading: Only one backbone (gpt-4-turbo) and one baseline family are tested; the only other memory-style comparison is STANDARD, which keeps everything.
All ablations are on Tyreworld alone, and §5.1 says removing both modules cuts success by 20 while Table 2 shows 30.0 (-30.0).
In the released code Blocksworld and Gripper skip the summarizer and show the last observation, which is the paper's 'w/o OS' heuristic; the paper does not mention this.
In code, a retrieve(...) output is itself sent to the environment as that step's action, so it uses one of the step budget and the follow-up LLM action is discarded.
The number of problems per task is not stated in the paper; the released configs list 20 Jericho games, up to 20 Gripper and Barman problems, and Tyreworld problem indices 2-9 (8 of 10).
Context and time are reported only as percentages of STANDARD, so absolute token or summarizer cost is not given.
